title: ⭐⭐ Practice: intentions, messages and the reason behind them

questions.prompt: Wassim and his father are watching the news when the electricity goes off. Wassim had not thought about the torch at all, but he stands up at once. Which sentence is the natural English for a decision taken at that very second?

options.text: I'm going to look for the torch.
I'm looking for the torch at eight.
I'll look for the torch.
I look for the torch every evening.

questions.explanation: "I'll look for the torch." is the natural one: will is the form English keeps for a decision born while you are speaking, and the scene says Wassim had not thought about the torch until the light went off. "I'm going to look for the torch." would mean the decision was already made before the electricity failed, which the situation rules out. "I'm looking for the torch at eight." is a present continuous of arrangement, as if Wassim had an appointment with his torch. And "I look for the torch every evening." is a present simple, so it describes a habit and says nothing about tonight.

questions.prompt: Join these two facts into one sentence. Cause: the lift in the block was out of order. Result: Emna climbed six floors with her shopping. Which sentence says it correctly?

options.text: The lift in the block was out of order, so Emna climbed six floors with her shopping.
Emna climbed six floors with her shopping, so the lift in the block was out of order.
The lift in the block was out of order because Emna climbed six floors with her shopping.
Emna climbed six floors with her shopping because of the lift was out of order.

questions.explanation: "The lift in the block was out of order, so Emna climbed six floors with her shopping." is right: so introduces the result, so the cause has to stand in front of it, and a comma goes before so when it joins two clauses. "Emna climbed six floors with her shopping, so the lift in the block was out of order." keeps the right linker but swaps the two facts, and ends up saying that the climb broke the lift. "The lift in the block was out of order because Emna climbed six floors with her shopping." reverses the relation the other way round, since because introduces the cause. And "Emna climbed six floors with her shopping because of the lift was out of order." puts a whole clause after because of, which only accepts a noun: either because the lift was out of order, or because of the broken lift.

questions.prompt: Three of these pairs say almost the same thing twice. In which pair do the two expressions mean the opposite of each other?

options.text: to renew a friendship — to start it again
an intimate friend — a very close friend
a faithful friend — a loyal friend
to keep in touch — to lose touch

questions.explanation: "to keep in touch — to lose touch" is the pair of opposites: keeping in touch means going on writing, phoning or meeting, while losing touch means being in contact no longer. "to renew a friendship — to start it again" says one thing twice, since to renew is precisely to start something again after a break. "an intimate friend — a very close friend" is another pair of near-synonyms: an intimate friend is the one you tell everything to. And "a faithful friend — a loyal friend" gives two words for the same quality, somebody who stays with you and never betrays you.

questions.prompt: Read this sentence: "Mouna's messages never reach her cousin, because he changed his number in March." What is the cause in this sentence?

options.text: Mouna's messages do not reach her cousin.
Her cousin changed his number in March.
Mouna does not write to her cousin any more.
Her cousin does not read his messages.

questions.explanation: "Her cousin changed his number in March." is the cause: because always introduces the reason, and everything that follows it here explains why the messages go astray. "Mouna's messages do not reach her cousin." is the result, the very fact that the cause explains, and the two must never be swapped. "Mouna does not write to her cousin any more." contradicts the sentence, which says she does write and that her messages do not arrive. And "Her cousin does not read his messages." invents a behaviour: the sentence blames a new number, not a lack of reading.

questions.prompt: The word "text" can be a noun or a verb. In which sentence is it used as a verb?

options.text: Text me when you get to Bizerte.
Her text was three lines long.
He sent me a text from the station.
I read your text twice this morning.

questions.explanation: "Text me when you get to Bizerte." uses text as a verb: it gives an order, it carries no article in front of it, and it is followed straight away by the person who receives the message. "Her text was three lines long." places the word after the possessive her, so it names a thing and it is a noun. "He sent me a text from the station." puts it after the article a, which only a noun accepts. And "I read your text twice this morning." makes it the object of the verb read, so once again it names a thing.

questions.prompt: Emna texts her cousin: "CU 2NITE B4 8, PLS." Which sentence writes her message in full?

options.text: Call you tonight before eight, please.
See you tomorrow night at eight, please.
See you tonight before eight, please.
Can you be there tonight at eight, please?

questions.explanation: "See you tonight before eight, please." is the full form: in a text message a letter stands for the word it sounds like, so C is see and U is you; a figure stands for the sound it makes, so 2NITE is tonight and B4 is before; and PLS is please with its vowels dropped. "Call you tonight before eight, please." reads C as call, but a letter only ever stands for the sound it makes, which is see. "See you tomorrow night at eight, please." turns 2NITE into tomorrow night and forgets that B4 means before, not at. And "Can you be there tonight at eight, please?" rebuilds a question that none of the shortcuts contains.
